title: Staged Fusion + Page-Aware FlashAttention Notes
content:
Purpose and context:

This is a working notes doc capturing experiments, heuristics, and design ideas for combining FlashAttention microkernels with a staged fusion approach that is aware of the paged (stripe) KV cache layout used in our paged-KV implementation. Goal is to reduce per-token latency and PCIe/GPU memory pressure while keeping register/shared-memory usage within occupancy sweet spots.

High level goals:
- Provide a kernel design that fuses QKV unpacking, attention compute (FlashAttention-style) and an optional lightweight output linear/projection to avoid writing large intermediate tensors back to global memory.
- Make the kernel paged-KV aware so it can avoid loading full past-kv pages when attention uses a small active window (recent tokens), enabling prefix caching optimizations.
- Keep multiple fallbacks: full-fusion (fast path), split-fusion (mixed), and reference paths for correctness.
- Provide scheduling heuristics for batching across requests and interleaving KV prefetch and attention compute to hide memory stalls.

Background summary (short):
- FlashAttention reduces global memory traffic by computing softmax over blocks in shared memory and streaming keys/values from global memory. It relies heavily on shared memory and warp-level cooperation.
- Our paged KV stores historical keys/values in pages (stripes) to allow eviction and efficient reuse. Pages can be resident GPU memory, CPU pinned, or remote; access cost varies.
- Naive fusion can increase register pressure and reduce occupancy, so we need staged fusion with multiple micro-variants chosen at runtime based on seq_len, batch, head_dim, and page residency.

Design overview: staged-fusion model
- Fast path (fully fused): Q project -> tile load of K/V (page-resident) -> FlashAttn block compute (warp-level softmax) -> fused output projection + write. Best when: head_dim <= 128, block_seq <= 512, KV pages resident on GPU, high throughput requirement.
- Mid path (staged): Q project + attention compute fused within each tile, but V accumulation and output projection done in a separate kernel to reduce register pressure. This allows streaming V pages and using less shared mem for partial reductions. Good for medium head_dim (128-256) or when some KV pages are on CPU pinned memory.
- Split path (fallback): separate kernels for matmul(q,k) then softmax then matmul with v. Used for very large head_dim or pathological occupancy/reg pressure cases and for correctness verification.

Key kernel-level strategies:
1) Page-aware prefetching
- Kernel queries the page table for K/V pages required by the request. If many pages are resident, use fused fast path. If some pages are non-resident, trigger async prefetch for those pages and start computing on resident pages (partial attention).
- For prefix attention (recent window), check mapping for contiguous recent pages — often only last 1-4 pages needed; avoid touching older pages.
- Prefetch policy: if miss_count/pages_needed < 0.25 and predicted remaining compute > threshold, prefetch and use staged path. Heuristic thresholds tuned via perf runs.

2) Block tiling and shared memory layout
- Tile size (T): choose based on head_dim and SM shared mem budget. Empirical sweet spots: head_dim 64 -> T=128 seq-block; head_dim 128 -> T=64; head_dim 256 -> T=32.
- Layout K and V in shared mem as transposed blocks to minimize bank conflicts when loads are performed across warps. Use padding to avoid 32-bank aliasing on 4-byte elements.
- Keep partial softmax accumulators in warp-level registers where possible; fall back to shared mem for larger block reductions.

3) Warp-cooperative streaming and KV eviction hints
- Kernel uses per-warp ring buffers to stream chunks of a KV page. Each warp issues a single global load for its chunk; cooperative loads aggregated via L2-friendly patterns.
- Emit eviction hints: if a page's last touch index < LRU_threshold and memory pressure high, mark page softly-evictable. This helps background eviction thread.

4) Quantization and fused dequant path
- For int8/4-bit KV pages we can fuse on-the-fly dequant into shared mem load to reduce intermediate memory writes. Keep scale/zero params per page in small per-page header cached in constant memory.
- Prefer staged path when dequant increases compute per element (we may need extra FLOPs).

5) Register pressure mitigation (staged fusion rationale)
- In fully fused path, spilling can happen when head_dim * (local accumulators + projection weights) exceeds registers/warp. To avoid this: break projection out of the hot loop; do accumulation in FP16 registers then do final projection in separate kernel.
- Also use loop unrolling factors tuned based on occupancy model (NVidia occupancy API) to balance registers vs latency.

Scheduling heuristics and runtime decisions
- Input features used to pick micro-variant: seq_len, batch_size, head_dim, pages_resident_fraction, latency_budget_ms, request_priority.
- Decision table (simplified):
  * pages_resident_fraction >= 0.9 and head_dim <= 128 -> fully fused fast path
  * pages_resident_fraction between 0.4 and 0.9, head_dim <= 256 -> staged fusion
  * otherwise -> split path or fallback (safety).
- Use a cheap estimator to compute expected memory stall time: stalls = non_resident_pages * avg_page_fetch_latency; if stalls < compute_time_estimate * 0.2 then do prefetch and run staged; else fall back.

KV-page-consistency and correctness notes
- When prefetching and computing on partial pages, ensure softmax normalization accounts for missing chunks. We implement attention as streaming reduction: compute per-chunk max/exp_sum, reduce maxima across chunks with atomic or warp-level combine, then compute normalized contributions. Watch for numerical issues with mixed residency.
- Provide a correctness-mode flag that forces split-path synchronous loads (slower) for test and regression.

Benchmarks and microresults (summary of runs on A100 40GB):
- Synthetic run: batch=8, heads=32, head_dim=64, seq=1024, pages_resident_fraction=1.0
  * fully fused: p95 per-token latency 3.6ms, GPU occupancy 48%, SM shared mem 34%
  * staged: p95 per-token latency 4.2ms, occupancy 62% (higher but more kernel launches)
- Mixed residency run: same settings but pages_resident_fraction=0.6, avg page fetch latency (pinned CPU) = 0.6ms
  * staged with prefetch: p95 5.8ms (prefetch overlapped), correctness verified vs reference
  * split path: p95 8.9ms

Memory and L2 traffic observations:
- Fully fused reduces global writes by ~42% in our synthetic kernels (no output projection case) compared to split path.
- Shared mem usage increases, but if head_dim small this is fine. Large head_dims push shared mem to kernel limit and reduce SM concurrency.

Implementation notes and API changes
- Kernel needs access to page table object and a fast page residency bitmap per-stream (a small per-stream structure in global memory). We should add a tiny page lookup kernel that fills a per-request residency bitmask before deciding kernel variant. That kernel is cheap (<100us) and avoids duplicating page checks in every block.
- Add a runtime-configured kernel selector in the C++ runtime (in serving-runtime/kernels) that queries batch-level features and decides variant. Expose debug flags to force variant.
- Error handling: if prefetch fails (OOM or IO error), fall back to split-path and mark request with tag for telemetry.

Open problems / questions:
- Numerical stability across partial reductions: streaming softmax variants are sensitive to chunk order. Need deterministic ordering or compensation for variance across runs.
- Interaction with CUDA Multi-Process Service (MPS) and how prefetching pins/pulls pages when multiple clients share device. Prefetch policy should be MPS-aware.
- How to handle V pages that are larger (double width due to quantization expansion). Our heuristics need to be quantization-scheme aware.
- Does fused projection always pay off for larger output dims (e.g., projection_dim > head_dim)? We need cost model.|

Short-term action items (owners assigned):
- Priya: implement per-request page residency bitmask kernel + kernel selector hooks (WIP). Target: 2024-12-09.
- Ethan: prototype fully fused variant that includes fused linear out; measure register pressure and occupancy across head_dims. Target: 2024-12-13.
- Maya: run mixed-residency microbenchmarks with pinned-CPU pages to get better latency distribution histograms; verify correctness for streaming softmax. Target: 2024-12-06.
- Diego: update pager eviction hint and telemetry event schema to capture page-touch heatmaps; expose to console. Target: 2024-12-18.

Notes to reviewers and checklist before shipping:
- Add unit tests for streaming-softmax numeric equivalence within tolerance.
- Add a stress test where pages are being evicted concurrently to ensure kernel correctness under race conditions.
- Audit shared mem usage per variant across supported GPU families (A100, H100, upcoming Gaudi?).
- Document runtime flags for forcing kernel variants and telemetry tags emitted on fallbacks/prefetches.

Quick sketches / pseudocode (staged flow):
- prefetch-check kernel (fast): fills residency_bitmap[pages_needed] and resident_count
- selector decides: if resident_count == pages_needed -> launch fully_fused_kernel else launch staged_kernel (with prefetch requests kicked off)

Fully fused kernel inner loop (conceptual):
for tile in seq_tiles:
  load Q_tile into registers
  for page_chunk in required_pages:
    cooperative_load K_chunk into shared_mem
    cooperative_load V_chunk into shared_mem
    compute_block_attn(Q_tile, K_chunk) // warp-level softmax fused
    accumulate_output_in_registers(V_chunk)
  apply_out_projection(register_accum)
  write_output

Staged kernel variant: similar but writes partial accumulators to global temp buffer after each page_chunk to reduce register pressure; final reduce kernel aggregates partials and runs projection.

Closing: this is experimental; the objective is to get a robust set of heuristics and a small number of well-optimized kernels rather than a combinatorial explosion of variants. We should measure telemetry and fold learned policy thresholds into runtime over time.
